passages.original: Vectes autem Damasci, quasi serae robustissimae atque firmissimae [Al. fortissi- mae), hi intelligantur, qui instructi sunt arte dia- lectica, et argumentis philosophorum. Verbi gratia : Ostium vocatur, qui falsum dogma concepit et peperit, ut Arius in Alexandria : vectes ejus et firmissimae serae ejus, Euticius 1 et Eunomius, qui syllogismis et enthymematibus, imo sophismatibus, et pseudomenis atque soritis, quae ab aliis male in- venta sunt, roborare conantur.
passages.english: Now let the bars of Damascus, like very strong and very firm bolts [another reading: very powerful], be understood as those who are equipped with the art of dialectic and with the arguments of the philosophers. For example: the one who conceived and gave birth to a false doctrine is called the door, as Arius in Alexandria; his bars and his very firm bolts are Eutychius and Eunomius, who try to strengthen [it] with syllogisms and enthymemes, or rather with sophisms, and 'liars' and sorites, which were wickedly devised by others.
passages.notes: "Euticius" is printed with a footnote mark; probably Eutychius (or possibly Euzoius, an Arian bishop); identification uncertain. "pseudomenis" refers to the 'Liar' paradox type of argument; "soritis" to the sorites (heap) argument.

passages.original: Et quia semel juxta leges tropologiae, Samaria refertur ad haere- ticos, qui custodes mandatorum Dei esse se men- tiuntur, praecipit sermo divinus, ut in gentibus praedicent, quae non habent notitiam Dei, in qua- rum doctrina ignis exurens est, et tribulatio et angustia : ut considerent falsam Samariam, et ascendant ad montes superbiae ejus, videant mul- tas insanias in medio civitatis, dum unusquisque fingit quod voluerit, et adorat figmentum suum : ut Marcion bonum Deum et otiosum : ut Valentinus αιώνας triginta, et extremum Christum, quem appellat, έκτρωμα, id est, abortivum : ut Basili- des, qui omnipotentem Deum portentoso nomine appellat *A€ράξας1, et eumdem secundum Grae- cas litteras, et annui cursus numerum dicit in so- lis circulo contineri, quem ethnici sub eodem numero aliarum litterarum vocant Μείϋραν.
passages.english: And since, once [we follow] the laws of tropology, Samaria is referred to the heretics, who falsely claim to be keepers of God's commandments, the divine word commands that they proclaim among the nations which have no knowledge of God, in whose teaching there is a burning fire, and tribulation and distress, that they should consider the false Samaria, and go up to the mountains of its pride, [and] see the many madnesses in the middle of the city, while each one invents whatever he wishes and worships his own invention: as Marcion [invents] a good and idle God; as Valentinus thirty aeons, and last of all Christ, whom he calls *ektrōma*, that is, an abortion; as Basilides, who calls the almighty God by the monstrous name Abraxas, and says that this same [god], according to the Greek letters and the number of the yearly course, is contained in the circle of the sun; him the pagans call Mithras, with the same number in other letters.
passages.notes: "*A€ράξας" is a scanning corruption of Abraxas (Ἀβράξας); "Μείϋραν" is a corruption of Μείθραν (Meithras/Mithras). Both names sum to 365 in Greek letter values.

passages.original: Et septem hebdomades complent numerum sanctae Pentecostes : et Jubilaeus annus remissionis tuba- rumque clangentium hoc numero texitur. In se- ptimo quoque mense figuntur tabernacula, et He braeus, cum sex annis servierit, anno septimo liberabi- tur 3. Novit et hoc saecularis philosophia et medicorum libri, quorum Galenus disertissimus atque doctissimus scripsit ternos libros κρίσεων* χα\4των κριτικών ήμερων, in quibus septenarii numeri ostendens potentiam, ardentissimas febres septimo dicit solvi die : aut si tanta humoris noxii et pituitae fuerit magnitudo, ut primae hebdomadis nequaquam fer- vore consumpta sit, secundae hebdomadis ultimus exspectatur dies, id est, quartus decimus. Quod si hunc, ut juxta Hippocratem loquar, νόσος vice- rit, transeunt ad vicesimam primam diem, hoc est, ad finem tertiae hebdomadis : ita ab initio mundi diebus conditis, ut omnes labores et molestiae septimo numero conquiescant.
passages.english: And seven weeks make up the number of holy Pentecost; and the Jubilee, the year of release and of sounding trumpets, is woven from this number. In the seventh month too the tabernacles are pitched, and the Hebrew, when he has served six years, will be set free in the seventh year. Secular philosophy also knows this, and the books of the physicians, of whom Galen, most eloquent and most learned, wrote three books each on crises and on critical days, in which, demonstrating the power of the number seven, he says that the most burning fevers are resolved on the seventh day; or, if the quantity of noxious humour and phlegm has been so great that it has by no means been consumed by the heat of the first week, the last day of the second week is awaited, that is, the fourteenth. But if, to speak in Hippocrates' terms, the disease (*nosos*) has overcome this [day], they pass to the twenty-first day, that is, to the end of the third week: the days having been so established from the beginning of the world that all labours and troubles come to rest in the number seven.
passages.notes: The Greek title is garbled in the scan (κρίσεων* χα\4των κριτικών ήμερων); read as περὶ κρίσεων καὶ περὶ κρισίμων ἡμερῶν, i.e. Galen's works 'On Crises' and 'On Critical Days', three books each ('ternos'). Footnote numerals omitted.

passages.original: Denique et capti- vitas populi Israel, templique subversio, septuage- simo anno desolationis impleta est, et septeni astra juxta numerum dierum dicuntur errantia 5. De cujus numeri sacramentis in Scipionis somnio plenius narrat Tullius : et obscurissimus Platonis Timaeus liber est 6, qui ne Ciceronis quidem aurea ore fit planior 7. Sicut igitur septenarius numeres habet sacramentum suum, sic sanctificatus atque perfectus, et ut ita dicam, verus est numerus, qui unione retinetur, et unius Dei majestate conclu- ditur [Al.
passages.english: Finally, the captivity of the people of Israel and the overthrow of the temple were completed in the seventieth year of desolation, and the seven stars are called 'wandering' according to the number of the days. Of the mysteries of this number Tully gives a fuller account in the Dream of Scipio; and Plato's Timaeus is a most obscure book, which is not made clearer even by Cicero's golden mouth. Just as, therefore, the number seven has its own mystery, so that number is sanctified and perfect, and, so to speak, true, which is held fast by unity and is enclosed in the majesty of the one God [another reading:
passages.notes: The passage ends mid-way in an editorial note of a variant reading ('[Al.' = alias), which continues in the following text ('recluctitur'), apparently a corrupt variant for 'concluditur'. 'numeres' read as 'numerus'; 'aurea ore' as printed (likely 'aureo ore'). Footnote numerals omitted.
